column3: Directly repeats the prohibition of calling another god alongside Allah and links it to punishment.
Frames rival claims at the final gathering as subject to demanded proof and exposed fabrication.
Its success formula supplies a positive counterpart to 23:117's denial of success to disbelievers.
Restates the ban on another god, then grounds exclusive judgment and return in Allah alone.
The immediate context rejects coexisting gods by showing that divided creation and dominance would follow.
Contrasts the verse's failed calling with a communal call toward good and away from wrong.
Reiterates not calling another god with Allah as a defining boundary of faithful conduct.
The preceding proclamation of the true King and sole god sets the sovereignty premise for 23:117.
Its retained contrast route only marks a boundary against displaced or divided orientation.
Connects fabricated claims about Allah and denial of signs with the outcome of no success.
Clarifies that each self is repaid for what it earned, sharpening 23:117's personal account.
Gives the punitive outcome for obstinate covering of truth, a boundary for the verse's no-success verdict.
Its contrast reading ties false attribution and denial of signs to failed success without selecting a positive route.
The immediate context names Allah knower of unseen and seen, then rejects what they associate.
Offers a secondary contrast between successful restraint and the verse's failed disbelief.
Forbids placing another god with Allah and shows the resulting abandonment and blame.
Identifies selective denial as genuine disbelief and attaches an abasing punishment.
Places hostile schemes within Allah's oversight, supporting the certainty of the account.
Shows the grave consequence of arriving before one's Lord as a criminal.
The nearby rhetorical question exposes the inconsistency after acknowledging Allah's claim.
Supplies the positive side: guidance from the Lord is joined to success.
Links the final outcome and lack of success to the distinction between guidance and wrongdoing.
Provides an explicit instance of proof from the Lord confronting a rebellious people.
Distinguishes a messenger's warning from control over signs, preserving Allah's sole authority.
Again forbids another god with Allah and attaches expulsion into punishment.
Its nearby contrast between human payment and the Lord's provision is only indirect context.
Shows recompense as located with the Lord, paralleling the account before one's Lord.
Sets final outcome and no success against wrongdoing, a secondary parallel to 23:117.
Questions whether earth-bound gods can give life, challenging the plausibility of rival gods.
Sets worship and good action as a positive route toward success.
Pairs a false expectation with finding Allah and receiving a complete account.
Nearby mention of signs and testing supplies only broad local context.
Treats the disbelievers' response to warning as rejection rather than a lack of warning.
Makes wrongdoing an acquisition borne by the self, complementing personal accounting.
The package-local branch relation does not add a clear reading of association, proof, account, or success.
Its measured celestial order supports the account motif only indirectly.
Links disbelief to lack of success after a corrective recognition of Allah's control.
Nearby affirmation of the Lord's signs offers limited context for the surrounding argument.
Defines resistance as persistence against signs, clarifying a boundary of disbelief.
Directly assigns the final account to Allah.
Demands proof for gods besides Allah and identifies turning away from the truth.
Presents disbelief as denying Allah's signs despite witness, making lack of proof not the issue.
Shows proof from the Lord actively turning a servant away from evil.
The nearby acknowledgment of Allah leads to a call for reverent response.
Names a proof from the Lord alongside a clarifying light.
Directly locates people's account with the Lord rather than human gatekeepers.
States the consistent messengerial proclamation of one god and exclusive worship.
Its source-from-Us wording has only a secondary relation to the verse's account before the Lord.
Commands sincere, unmixed devotion directed to Allah despite disbelievers' objection.
Its successful weighing supplies a nearby positive counterpart to no success in 23:117.
Contrasts narrowed worldly aim with Allah's encompassing recompense, only indirectly relevant.
Names the addressed group as disbelievers, a limited aid to the final designation in 23:117.
Its desired final abode and reward provide only a distant positive contrast.
Sets faith against disbelief, defiance, and disobedience as competing moral orientations.
Joins creation, return, provision, rival-god challenge, and demand for proof in one argument.
The nearby call to a straight path contrasts with calling another god.
Forbids calling anyone with Allah in the setting of worship spaces.
Does not clearly add to association, proof, account, or the no-success conclusion.
Reserves unseen knowledge to Allah, setting a limit on rival claims.
States that Allah knows what is called besides Him, making false invocation fully answerable.
Pairs avoidance of idols with avoidance of false speech, supporting the verse's rejection of unsupported association.
The nearby acknowledgment of Allah is followed by a demand for reflection.
Portrays rejection of what is from Allah as deep estrangement, a boundary for disbelief.
Its Lord-pleasing conduct gives only a broad positive contrast.
The branch route supplies a secondary contrast in which resistance prevents wrongful action.
Establishes non-transferable personal burden, clarifying whose account is at stake.
Contrasts a truthful standing with the disbelievers' accusation of sorcery.
Nearby commands to messengers offer broad ethical context only.
Places speech-action inconsistency under Allah's grave evaluation, a secondary account boundary.
Its self-directed striving is only indirectly related to individual accountability.
The branch route offers a secondary example of the Lord diverting harmful intent.
Treats disbelief as a persistent collective condition with severe consequence.
Shows an inescapable summons, supporting the certainty of the later account.
Shows leaders dismissing a messenger through status-driven denial, illuminating disbelief in the surah's argument.
Describes persistent disbelief as blocking faith, a boundary for the verse's final category.
Its gratitude-versus-disbelief test offers only a secondary contrast.
The retained contrast route marks that deniers cannot evade the summoned day.
Separates the messenger's duty of delivery from Allah's duty of account.
Its delayed treatment of disbelievers supplies only a distant consequence context.
Warning an obstinate people gives only general context for the verse's call and judgment.
Offers a positive path toward success through reverence, seeking means to Allah, and striving.
Defines denial of signs as knowing rejection, sharpening the sense of disbelief.
Links successful outcome to true weighing, a positive counterpart to 23:117's no success.
Condemns speaking without knowledge and measures it as grave with Allah, supporting the proof boundary.
Shows rejection after the sought reminder arrives, clarifying culpable disbelief.
Explicitly forbids making another god with Allah and frames it as the subject of warning.
Reserves knowledge to Allah while preserving the messenger's clear warning role.
Treats seeking an alternative way as unaccepted and ending in loss.
Places disbelievers' deeds under recompense, supporting the account-and-consequence frame.
Restates making another god with Allah and directly joins it to severe punishment.
Denies any protector from Allah on the day of turning away, reinforcing inescapable accountability.
States that fabricators against Allah do not succeed.
Its uncrossed boundary offers only a formal contrast to crossing the limit of exclusive devotion.
Commands the prophet not to obey disbelievers and hypocrites, marking a directional boundary.
Names Allah as the sole god and king, then declares transcendence above association.
Links entering punishment to prior disbelief.
Shows a false claim brought under divine retribution from beginning to end.
Contrasts Allah's sovereign control with the utter lack of possession of those called besides Him.
Shows self-wronging as the cause of ruined investment, a secondary analogy for failed outcome.
Its contrast of worldly play with the lasting final abode only broadly supports the account horizon.
Requires proof for an exclusive salvific claim, directly reinforcing 23:117's demand for proof.
Places earned recompense under Allah's swift account.
Affirms Allah's sole divinity and unchallenged sovereignty, grounding rejection of a rival god.
Makes all hidden and manifest contents answerable to Allah's reckoning.
Joins divine witness, knowledge, justice, and the declaration that there is no god except Him.
States that associating partners with Allah is not forgiven, marking the gravity of 23:117's act.
Repeats the unforgiven character of associating partners and its far deviation.
Rejects deifying the Messiah and attaches exclusion from the garden to association.
Rejects the claim of three and insists on one god, with warning of punishment.
Sets the Qur'an's warning against claims of another god with Allah.
Foretells the exposure of those whom associators claimed as partners.
Forbids worshiping those called besides Allah and distinguishes the revealed guidance.
Questions turning to what neither benefits nor harms besides Allah.
Names the error of making jinn partners with Allah despite His creating them.
Commands following revelation from the Lord and turning away from associators.
Forbids associating with Allah what He has not authorized and speaking without knowledge.
Challenges claimed partners by asking whether they create anything.
Denies that those called besides Allah can answer their callers.
Condemns taking religious authorities as lords besides Allah against exclusive worship.
Describes worship besides Allah without harm or benefit and exposes unsupported intercession claims.
Portrays the final separation of associators from their alleged partners.
Shows that those invoked besides Allah neither help nor avert the divine decree.
Contrasts Allah's true call with the nonresponse of those called besides Him.
Links assigning rivals to Allah with misguidance from His way.
States that those called besides Allah create nothing and are themselves created.
Forbids taking two gods and affirms that He alone is one god.
Challenges those called besides Allah as unable to remove or transfer harm.
Denies Allah any partner in dominion and any need of a protector.
Demands clear authority for taking gods besides Allah and calls unsupported attribution grave wrongdoing.
States that people take gods besides Allah seeking might, preparing the reversal of that reliance.
Affirms that the only god is Allah, whose knowledge encompasses all things.
Argues that multiple gods in heaven and earth would have brought corruption.
Questions whether any gods besides Allah can protect their worshipers.
Describes calling besides Allah what cannot harm or benefit as manifest error.
Contrasts Allah as the true reality with the falsehood of what is called besides Him.
Condemns worship without revealed authority or knowledge.
Describes taking gods besides Allah that create nothing and lack control over life, death, and resurrection.
Describes worship besides Allah what neither benefits nor harms.
Challenges whether any god is with Allah in the work of creation and provision.
Challenges whether any god is with Allah in ordering the earth and waters.
Challenges whether any god is with Allah in answering the distressed and removing harm.
Challenges whether any god is with Allah in guidance through darkness and sending mercy.
Affirms that He is Allah with no god except Him and that judgment belongs to Him.
Denies that those worshiped besides Allah control provision and directs provision-seeking to Allah.
Denies intercessors among alleged partners and records their disavowal.
Connects creation, provision, death, and life to Allah, then challenges any partner's share in these acts.
Names association with Allah as great wrongdoing.
Contrasts Allah as the true reality with the falsehood of what is called besides Him.
States that alleged partners possess nothing in the heavens or earth and have no share or support.
Restricts intercession to Allah's permission, limiting claimed mediating powers.
Challenges whether any creator besides Allah provides from heaven and earth, then affirms no god except Him.
States that those called besides Allah do not hear and will disavow association on the Day of Resurrection.
Rejects taking gods besides Allah whose intercession cannot help against divine harm.
Describes taking gods besides Allah in hope of help, setting up their inability.
Rejects devotion to protectors besides Allah and reserves judgment over their disputes to Him.
Exposes the inconsistency of affirming Allah as creator while invoking others for harm and mercy.
Warns that association nullifies deeds and ends in loss.
States that every self is paid in full for what it did, directly expanding the account motif.
Explains punishment through rejecting belief in Allah alone while accepting association with Him.
Affirms Allah's judgment in truth against those invoked besides Him who judge nothing.
Contrasts calling to Allah with calling to one lacking effective response in this world and the next.
Declares that what is called to has no effective call and that return is to Allah.
Asks whether any gods besides the Most Merciful were appointed for worship.
Names Him God in heaven and God on earth, grounding undivided sovereignty.
Demands evidence of what alleged partners created or share in, and calls for a prior record or trace of knowledge.
Calls those who invoke besides Allah astray because their objects cannot answer until resurrection.
States that the invoked objects will become enemies and reject their worship.
Asks whether they have a god other than Allah and declares His transcendence above association.
Begins the critique of named female deities, providing a direct rival-god context.
Affirms Allah's sole divinity and knowledge of unseen and seen, closely paralleling 23:92-117.
Affirms Allah as the only god and directs trust to Him.
Declares worship and calling directed to the Lord without associating anyone with Him.
Denies personal power over harm or right guidance, reinforcing exclusive divine authority.
Provides a direct positive counterpart: one who receives a record will face an easy account.
Explicitly names the easy account, clarifying that accounting is an eschatological encounter.
